title: At 17, Indian American Kairav Mittal Is Bringing Yoga to Rural Virginia
excerpt: Through Project Root in Crewe, the teenager who took up yoga at 12 is teaching breathwork to his neighbours, building a free pranayama app, and launching children's classes in a town residents call a health desert
body:
• Kairav Mittal, 17, teaches free yoga in Crewe, in Southside Virginia, through his initiative Project Root.
  • He began yoga at 12, initially reluctantly, and decided to teach after summers working in Crewe showed him the town's limited access to health and wellness facilities.
  • Classes have grown by word of mouth from three or four people to nine, and a new Yoga for Young Roots programme will serve children ages 3 to 12.
  • His free RootBreath pranayama app extends the classes to anyone who cannot attend in person.

At 17, Kairav Mittal is turning a practice he once resisted into a community resource. The Indian American teenager teaches yoga in Crewe, Virginia, through Project Root, which he created to make breathing, mindfulness and movement more accessible in a town with few wellness resources, The American Bazaar reported in an exclusive interview.

Mittal began practising yoga at 12, under Master Kamal, who teaches in the Himalayan tradition. "As a 12-year-old, I didn't find much value in it and thought it was a waste of time," he said. "But as I became more consistent and practiced every day, I began to experience the benefits of yoga and mindfulness, [which became] the reason I wanted to teach it."

Why he chose Crewe

Mittal's connection to Crewe was built over several summers — working in food service at a restaurant there, then, two summers ago, interning at the town hall. "There's no central gym and no open space to talk about feelings and health," he said. "Crewe has given me a lot, so I thought I should give something back."

Jess, who has lived in Crewe for 14 years, described the community as a "health desert" and said Project Root could offer stress relief, physical activity and mental health support. After a class, she felt "refreshed and relaxed" and planned to return. David Clements said the practice helps people understand their bodies and breathing.

Small classes, growing by word of mouth

Teaching at 17 was nerve-wracking at first, Mittal admitted. Attendance, though, has grown steadily: "I only had about three or four people and then, the next week that turned into six, and the week after that turned into nine." Progress, he emphasised, is not mastering difficult poses. By week seven, he noted, regulars who had struggled simply sit more comfortably during seated breathwork, — and they keep showing up.

Town officials have backed the effort. "We're grateful to Kairav for volunteering his time and talents to offer yoga classes to Crewe's young people," said Phil Miscovic, Crewe's town manager, linking it to the town's Virginia Foundation for Healthy Youth grant and HEAL Crewe initiative.

Breath first, then an expansion to children

Mittal insists the biggest misconception about yoga is that it is all about postures. "Breath is the key," he said, arguing that breathing in and out at the right moments matters as much as any stretch. That emphasis shaped RootBreath, the free pranayama app he built at rootbreath.org so people can practise whenever they choose.

The next step is Yoga for Young Roots, a monthly programme for children ages 3 to 12, organised with the Town of Crewe and the Nottoway County Library System and supported by a Healthy Communities Action Team grant from the Virginia Foundation for Healthy Youth. Sessions, capped at 12 children, will combine breathing, simple poses and relaxation. The foundation's Healthy Communities Action Teams programme funds local collaboratives that promote healthy behaviours including moving more and reducing stress with increased mindfulness — the behaviours those sessions are designed to build.

Mittal also hopes a young teacher helps undo a stigma: younger people who assume yoga is only for older adults, and older people who do not want to be seen that way. "Yoga is for everyone," he said. Project Root, he stressed, is not a one-summer project — he wants to bring the model to other communities like Crewe.
